name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say is linked to your name. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an 18-tonne box lorry for an appliance and furniture retailer, and I've got a crewmate, Kofi, in the passenger seat. We deliver washing machines, fridges and sofas, and we plumb in the washers and take the old ones away. Ten or eleven homes a day, all different, all with stairs. I love the puzzle of getting an American fridge through a narrow door, honestly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Sam, my partner, in a rented flat by the ring road. Sam picks orders at the big online retailer's warehouse on nights. We've got less than a month of bills saved. I use AI every day, for writing listings for old appliances I fix up and sell on weekends, and for working out routes when the office gets it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd probably post that it's still useful even if it's not magic. I use it every day and it saves me an hour a week. People who said it'd change everything were overselling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as it is, which is fine but tight. Money's the problem, not robots. The retailer pays less than the supermarkets, and there aren't many other lorry jobs close by. My weekend appliance sales are what make the rent work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and grow the weekend side hustle, maybe to two or three fridges a month instead of one. I'd look at a proper appliance repair course, so I can fix more than washers. I'd keep using AI to write the listings and price things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit restless, because I want more than just getting by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend side hustle.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People are always happy for us to take the old washer away. Some of the old washing machines people throw away just need a new pump or belt. I fix one in the shed at Sam's mum's, list it online, and make a bit on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your employer know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not officially. The manager's turned a blind eye so far. If they asked me to stop, I'd have to think hard about which one pays better.

People who promised it would change everything were **overselling** it.
think: The job stays, but **money** stays tight on a lower-paid retailer wage.
My weekend **appliance sales** are what make the rent work.
do: Grow the **side hustle** to two or three fridges a month.
Look at an **appliance repair course** to fix more types.
Keep using **AI for listings** and pricing.
feel: Mostly **okay**, a bit **restless** for more than getting by.

steps.text: Grow the weekend appliance resale to three fridges a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good news if you learn the tools. I'd post tips on how to use AI for small businesses, because I already do. Some of my mates would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is mostly hands-on, so I'd be fine for a while. The booking, the customer calls and the route planning would go to AI, and the office staff would shrink. But I worry about Sam, whose warehouse is already putting in picking robots. If my partner's night shifts at the warehouse go, we're on my wage and the side hustle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the side hustle harder and maybe get it registered properly, with a small website. I'd help Sam look at other jobs, maybe the forklift ticket. And I'd learn whatever new booking app the retailer uses, fast, so I'm the one they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about Sam. For me it feels like more chances than threats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not wait for the warehouse to decide for us. We'd look at courses together, maybe Sam does the forklift ticket or joins me on the repair side. I'd say it nicely, but I'd say it soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two women in the office who do the customer calls and bookings. One of them, Jan, has been there since the shop opened. AI would do her job in a week.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for anyone willing to learn the tools.
I'd post **AI tips** for people running small businesses on the side.
think: My **hands-on** job is safe for a while.
Sam's warehouse already has **picking robots**, which threatens our household.
do: Register the **side hustle** properly with a small website.
Help Sam get a **forklift ticket** or join the repair side.
Learn the retailer's new **booking app** fast.
feel: **Uneasy** about Sam, but seeing more **chances than threats** for herself.

fieldNote: Rosa sees the **office staff** and her partner's warehouse job hit first.

Her optimism about tools is real, but her **household risk** isn't small.

steps.text: Register the appliance resale business and build a small website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to adapt fast and the government needs to help people do it. I'd share practical advice online, not doom. But I'd be honest that it's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the office goes by 2028, and around 2031 robots could carry the fridges and plumb in the washers. Sam's warehouse would be gone even earlier, probably. Two years is very little time when you've got under a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on repairs, because fixing a broken thing in someone's kitchen is messy and different every time. I'd take an electrical course this year and build the repair business at weekends. I'd ask Sam's mum if we could move in to save rent while we build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I'd be busy, which helps. I'm better when I'm doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Repairs are hands-on too. Robots arrive around 2031. Why would repairs last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every repair is different: weird old pipes, a cat behind the machine, a customer who wants to chat. I think deliveries go first because they're the same thing ten times a day. Repairs might buy me a few more years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the three years between the AGI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use AI for everything on the business side, so I can run it alone: bookings, invoices, adverts. Then I just do the hands-on part. By 2031 I'd want a full diary of repair jobs.

say: I'd say we must **adapt fast** with government help.
I'd share **practical advice** online while admitting it's scary.
think: Office goes by **2028**, deliveries around **2031**, Sam's warehouse even earlier.
**Two years** is very little with under a month saved.
do: Ask **Sam's mum** about moving in to save rent.
S2.quote: Every repair is different: weird old pipes, a cat behind the machine, a customer who wants to chat.
fieldNote: Rosa splits her own job into **deliveries** that go first and **repairs** that may last.
She'd use AI to run the **business side** alone while doing hands-on work.

steps.text: Take an electrical course this year for appliance repairs
Build the weekend repair business with AI handling bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start if you take it seriously. I'd tell people to start learning a trade now and use AI to help them learn. That's practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the office changes by 2031 and the lorry around 2034. I could build a proper repair business in that time. The risk is that everyone else has the same idea, and I don't have savings to ride out a slow year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical course over two years and grow the repair side to three days a week by year three. I'd keep driving on the other days for steady money. Sam and I would save a little each month into a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more excited than scared. It feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the business fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad winter, a van breaking down, or a big firm sending robot repair crews around cheaper. I'd keep my driving licence current just in case. A fallback is a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does Sam fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's good with customers and hates nights. Maybe Sam does the second-hand sales and I do the fixing. We've talked about it half-joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to set up something better than what we have now. I'd post about how to start a small business with AI tools. People listen more when there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2039, I've got years of driving, and years to build the repair business slowly. I'd be fine if I don't waste it. Sam's job is the bigger risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep driving and do the repair course part-time. I'd keep the side hustle going and save the profits. I'd get Sam into a course too, without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly hopeful. It's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in this area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. There aren't many lorry jobs, but people everywhere have broken washing machines. A repair business can work in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any downside to so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfy. I'd set myself dates, like having a business bank account by next summer. Otherwise ten years becomes nine, then eight.

**Sam's job** is the bigger risk for us.

fieldNote: Ten years turns Rosa's worry into a **steady build-up** of her own business.
She guards against **complacency** by setting dated goals.

Keep driving the box lorry with Kofi

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I would both be hit with no savings. What would help is small-business grants and cheap evening courses, so drivers can turn hands-on skills into their own work. And rent help in the first year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether people have something on the side already. Lots of drivers do a bit of fixing, selling or odd jobs. That's where the new work could come from, if someone helped it grow.
